explanation:
Maybe because of the antenna's direction, the TV reception is poor.

---

- **アンテナ** — antenna (n). From English "antenna." In Japanese, also used metaphorically for one's sensitivity or awareness (アンテナを張る "keep one's antennas up"). [N2]
- **向（む）き** — direction, orientation (n). From verb 向く. [N3]
- **せいか** — because of, due to (conj). Expresses a negative cause; often implies blame. Related to せい (fault/responsibility). [N3]
- **映（うつ）り** — reception, image quality (n). From verb 映る [自動詞, counterpart: 映す 他動詞] "to be reflected/projected." [N3]
- **〜のか** — whether/doubt marker. Here softens the causal claim: "maybe it's because of X that…" [N3]

There are many young people listening to music with earphones on the train.

---

- **イヤホン** — earphone(s) (n). From English "earphone." Japanese often prefers this over ヘッドホン (headphones) for in-ear types. [N2]
- **電車（でんしゃ）の中（なか）** — inside the train. Note: Japanese uses 電車 for commuter trains in general, not strictly electric vs. diesel. [N5]
- **つけて** — attaching, putting on (te-form). From つける [他動詞, counterpart: つく 自動詞] "to attach/put on." Here: putting earphones in one's ears. [N5]
- **若者（わかもの）** — young people (n). Wago (和語) reading; the kanji 若者 can also be read as じゃくしゃ (kango, more formal). [N3]
- **〜ている** — progressive state. Describes an ongoing habitual scene, not a single action. [N5]

The factory's noon siren went off.

---

- **工場（こうじょう）** — factory (n). Kango (漢語). [N4]
- **サイレン** — siren (n). From English "siren" (ultimately Greek σειρήν). In Japan, factory and disaster-prevention sirens are common; the noon siren (昼のサイレン) is a well-known cultural feature in many towns. [N2]
- **お昼（ひる）** — noon, lunchtime (n). お- is a polite prefix (wago). [N5]
- **鳴（な）った** — sounded, went off (past). From 鳴る [自動詞, counterpart: 鳴らす 他動詞] "to sound/ring." Used for alarms, bells, sirens. [N4]
- Note: Japanese 鳴る covers a wider range of "sound-making" than English — it applies to instruments, animals, alarms, and phones.

I plugged the iron's cord into the outlet.

---

- **アイロン** — iron (for clothes) (n). From English "iron." Often appears as アイロンをかける (to iron clothes). [N2]
- **コード** — cord, cable (n). From English "cord." In Japanese, also means chord (music), code (programming). [N2]
- **コンセント** — electrical outlet (n). From "concentric plug" — a Japanese coinage not used in English (English: outlet, socket). [N2]
- **つないだ** — connected, plugged in (past). From つなぐ [他動詞, counterpart: つながる 自動詞] "to connect." [N3]

In the security room, there is a monitor showing the building's interior.

---

- **警備室（けいびしつ）** — security room, guard room (n). 警備 (security, kango) + 室 (room). [N2]
- **モニター** — monitor (n). From English "monitor." Can be a noun (display screen) or suru-verb (to monitor/observe). In IT contexts, often written as モニタ (shortened). [N2]
- **建物内部（たてものないぶ）** — building interior. 建物 (building) + 内部 (interior, kango). [N3]
- **映（うつ）す** — to show, project, reflect (noun-modifying form). 他動詞, counterpart: 映る 自動詞. [N3]
- **〜には…がある** — "in X there is Y." Existential construction. [N5]

Looking at the meter, you can tell the electricity and gas usage.

---

- **メーター** — meter (measuring device) (n). From English "meter." タクシーメーター (taxi meter) is a common compound. [N2]
- **見（み）る** — to look at (noun-modifying form). 他動詞. [N5]
- **電気（でんき）** — electricity (n). Also means "electric light." [N5]
- **ガス** — gas (n). From Dutch "gas" (ultimately Greek). Town gas and LPG are both called ガス in Japanese. [N3]
- **使用量（しりょう）** — amount of usage (n). Kango. 使用 (use) + 量 (quantity). [N2]
- **わかる** — to understand, be able to tell (dictionary form). 自動詞. Note: the subject of わかる is the thing understood, not the person (〜がわかる). [N5]

Men and women formed pairs and played a game.

---

- **男女（だんじょ）** — men and women (n). Kango. 男 (man) + 女 (woman). [N3]
- **ペア** — pair (n). From English "pair." ペアになる (to pair up / form a pair) is a fixed expression. Japanese uses ペア more broadly than English — e.g., ペアの靴下 (pair of socks). [N2]
- **なって** — becoming, forming (te-form). From なる [自動詞] "to become." ペアになる = "to become a pair." [N5]
- **ゲーム** — game (n). From English "game." Can refer to sports, video games, or party games. [N5]

The rhythm of this piece of music is in 3/4 time.

---

- **曲（きょく）** — piece of music, song (n). Counter for musical pieces. [N4]
- **リズム** — rhythm (n). From English "rhythm." In Japanese, also used metaphorically: リズムに乗る (get into the rhythm), リズムが崩れる (lose one's rhythm). [N2]
- **3拍子（さんびょうし／さんぱくし）** — 3-beat time, triple meter (n). 拍子 means "beat/time signature." The reading varies; in music contexts, さんびょうし is common. [N2]
- **〜だ** — copula. Plain form declarative. [N5]
- Note: Japanese rhythm terminology borrows heavily from Western music; 拍子 itself is a traditional Japanese musical term repurposed for Western notation.

The accent of "おかあさん" is on the "か" syllable.

---

- **アクセント** — accent, stress (n). From English "accent." In Japanese linguistics, refers specifically to pitch accent (高低アクセント), not stress accent. This is a key difference from English. [N2]
- **音（おと）** — sound, syllable (n). Here refers to a mora/syllable in the word. [N4]
- **ある** — to exist, be located (dictionary form). 自動詞. Indicates where the accent "falls." [N5]
- Note: Japanese has pitch accent (高低アクセント) — a binary high/low pattern per mora — which is fundamentally different from the stress-based accent of English or the tone system of Mandarin Chinese. Chinese speakers should be careful not to confuse these systems.

At the library, English books are arranged in alphabetical order.

---

- **図書館（としょかん）** — library (n). Kango. [N4]
- **アルファベット** — alphabet (n). From English "alphabet." In Japanese, specifically refers to the Latin/Roman alphabet, not kana or other scripts. Sometimes shortened to アルファ. [N2]
- **順（じゅん）** — order, sequence (n). Kango. アルファベットの順 = "in alphabetical order." [N3]
- **並（なら）べてある** — are arranged (te-form + ある). From 並べる [他動詞, counterpart: 並ぶ 自動詞] + auxiliary ある indicating a prepared state (結果の状態). Someone arranged them and they remain so. [N4]

I exchanged email addresses with my friend.

---

- **友（とも）だち** — friend (n). Wago. The だち suffix is a nominalizer meaning "companion." [N5]
- **メール** — email (n). From English "mail." In Japanese, メール almost always means email (not physical mail, which is 手紙 or 郵便). [N3]
- **アドレス** — address (n). From English "address." In modern Japanese, commonly means email address or URL. Physical addresses are 住所 (じゅうしょ). [N2]
- **交換（こうかん）** — exchange (n). Kango. Suru-verb: 交換する. [N3]
- Note: The Chinese false friend here is that アドレス does NOT mean "speech/address" (演讲) in Japanese — for that, use 講演（こうえん）.

I make a note of important things on paper.

---

- **大事（だいじ）** — important (na-adj). Kango. 大切（たいせつ） is a near synonym but more emotional ("precious"). [N4]
- **紙（かみ）** — paper (n). Wago. 紙にメモする = "note on paper." [N5]
- **メモ** — memo, note (n). From English "memo" (memorandum). Functions as both noun and suru-verb: メモする (to take notes). メモ帳 (notepad) is a common compound. [N2]
- Note: In Japanese, メモ implies a brief, informal note. For formal minutes or records, use 記録（きろく）or 議事録（ぎじろく）.

I put marks on the important points in a text to help memorize them.

---

- **文章（ぶんしょう）** — text, sentence, passage (n). Kango. 文 (sentence) + 章 (chapter). [N3]
- **重要（じゅうよう）な** — important (na-adj). Kango. Slightly more formal than 大事. [N3]
- **ポイント** — point, key point (n). From English "point." In Japanese, often used for key items or essential elements. [N2]
- **マーク** — mark (n/v). From English "mark." マークを付ける (to mark/put a mark on) is a fixed collocation. [N2]
- **覚（おぼ）える** — to memorize, remember (noun-modifying form). 他動詞, counterpart: 覚える is both transitive and intransitive depending on context; the counterpart for "to forget" is 忘（わす）れる. [N5]

This book has lots of illustrations, making the content easy to understand.

---

- **イラスト** — illustration (n). From English "illustration," shortened. Full form イラストレーション also exists but is rare. In Japanese, イラスト specifically means a drawn/painted illustration (not a photograph). イラストレーター (illustrator) is the profession. [N2]
- **たくさん** — many, a lot (adv). Wago. [N5]
- **内容（ないよう）** — content (n). Kango. [N3]
- **理解（りかい）しやすい** — easy to understand (i-adj). 理解 (understanding, kango) + する + やすい (easy to). The suffix やすい attaches to verb stem to mean "easy to X." [N3]
- **〜てある** — resulting state. 置いてある implies someone placed them there intentionally. (This pattern appears in the next entry's grammar, but here the structure is 〜て + 理解しやすい.)
- Note: Japanese イラスト has a strong association with anime/manga-style art. In academic or formal contexts, 図（ず）or 図表（ずひょう）is preferred.

I sign a contract.

---

- **契約書（けいやくしょ）** — contract (document) (n). Kango. 契約 (contract) + 書 (document). [N2]
- **サイン** — signature, signing (n/v). From English "sign." サインする = to sign. Note: In Japanese, サイン can also mean an autograph (有名人のサイン) or a hand signal (baseball). [N2]
- **する** — to do (dictionary form). 他動詞. Used here as suru-verb with サイン. [N5]
- Note: The Chinese false friend — サイン does NOT mean "sign" as in road sign (標識 ひょうしき) or mathematical symbol (記号 きごう). For autograph, Japanese also uses 署名（しょめい）in formal contexts.

When the movie became a hit, the lead actor quickly became a world-famous star.

---

- **映画（えいが）** — movie (n). Kango. [N5]
- **ヒット** — hit (n). From English "hit." ヒットする (to be a hit/success). [N2]
- **し** — te-form classical/literary variant. From する. Here used as a conditional/temporal connector: "when X happened, Y followed." Equivalent to して. [N3]
- **主演俳優（しゅえんはいゆう）** — lead actor (n). Kango. 主演 (lead role) + 俳優 (actor). [N2]
- **たちまち** — instantly, in no time (adv). Wago. Emphasizes rapid change. [N2]
- **世界的（せかいてき）な** — world-scale, global (na-adj). Kango + 的. [N3]
- **スター** — star (n). From English "star." Refers to a celebrity or famous person, not an astronomical object (which is 星 ほし). [N2]
- **なった** — became (past). From なる [自動詞] "to become." [N5]

In response to the audience's encore, the performers appeared on stage and greeted them.

---

- **観客（かんきゃく）** — audience, spectators (n). Kango. 観 (observe) + 客 (guest). [N2]
- **アンコール** — encore (n). From French "encore" (meaning "again"). In Japanese, refers to the audience's demand for a repeat performance, or the repeat performance itself. [N2]
- **こたえて** — responding to (te-form). From 応える/答える [他動詞] "to respond." Here: to respond to a request/demand. [N2]
- **出演者（しゅつえんしゃ）** — performers, cast (n). Kango. 出演 (appearance in a performance) + 者 (person). [N2]
- **舞台（ぶたい）** — stage (n). Kango. Also means "theatrical performance" metaphorically. [N3]
- **あいさつ** — greeting, address (n). From 挨拶. In this context, the performers give a post-show address/thanks to the audience. [N3]
- Note: アンコール is a French loanword that entered English first, then Japanese. The French original "encore" literally means "still/again."

She works as a fashion show model.

---

- **ファッションショー** — fashion show (n). From English "fashion show." Often shortened to ファッション or コレ (from collection) in industry slang. [N2]
- **モデル** — model (n). From English "model." In Japanese, covers: (1) fashion model, (2) role model (手本 てほん is the wago equivalent), (3) model number/prototype. [N2]
- **している** — is doing, works as (te-form + iru). する [他動詞] used for occupation/role. 〜をしている = "works as." [N5]
- Note: Japanese モデル for "fashion model" is a narrower usage than English. For "model student," Japanese uses 模範生（もはんせい）, not モデル.

There are food samples displayed at the entrance of the restaurant.

---

- **食堂（しょくどう）** — restaurant, cafeteria, dining hall (n). Kango. [N3]
- **入（い）り口** — entrance (n). Wago. 入口 can also be read as にゅうこう (kango, more formal). [N4]
- **料理（りょうり）** — dish, cuisine, cooking (n). Kango. [N4]
- **サンプル** — sample (n). From English "sample." In Japanese, specifically refers to the plastic/wax food replicas displayed outside restaurants (食品サンプル shokuhin sampuru), a uniquely Japanese custom. Also used for product samples, data samples. [N2]
- **置（お）いてある** — is placed (resulting state). From 置く [他動詞, counterpart: 置かれる (passive)] + auxiliary ある. Indicates someone placed it and it remains. [N5]
- Cultural note: 食品サンプル (food replicas) are a famous Japanese craft tradition, especially associated with Kappabashi (Tokyo) and Gujo Hachiman (Gifu).

She has a very good figure.

---

- **スタイル** — figure, physique; style (n). From English "style." Semantic drift: in Japanese, スタイルがいい specifically means "to have a good figure/body proportions" (not just "stylish"). This meaning is uniquely Japanese — English "style" does not carry this bodily connotation. [N2]
- **とても** — very (adv). Wago. [N5]
- **いい** — good (i-adj). [N5]
- Note: This is a classic example of 和製英語 (wasei eigo / Japanese-made English). English "style" means manner/fashion, but Japanese スタイル meaning "body proportions" derives from the English phrase "good style" in a physical sense. For "style" in the English sense (fashion, manner), Japanese may use スタイル or 風格（ふうかく）depending on context.

I've gained weight recently and the waist of my skirt has gotten tight.

---

- **最近（さいきん）** — recently (adv/n). Kango. [N4]
- **太（ふと）って** — having gained weight (te-form). From 太る [自動詞, counterpart: 太らせる 他動詞] "to get fat/gain weight." [N3]
- **スカート** — skirt (n). From English "skirt." [N3]
- **ウエスト** — waist (n). From English "waist" (via the anatomical term). In Japanese, ウエスト also refers to waist measurement (ウエストがきつい = "tight at the waist"). [N2]
- **きつく** — tight, snug (adverbial form). From きつい (i-adj). Here describes clothing that is too tight. [N3]
- **なった** — became (past). From なる [自動詞] "to become." [N5]
- Note: Japanese uses multiple body-part loanwords for measurements: ウエスト (waist), ヒップ (hips), バスト (bust). These are standard in clothing size contexts.

The calories needed per day by an adult male are said to be about 1,800-2,000 kcal.

---

- **成人男性（せいせいんだんせい）** — adult male (n). Kango. 成人 (adult) + 男性 (male). [N2]
- **1日（いちにち）** — one day, per day (n). [N5]
- **必要（ひつよう）な** — necessary (na-adj). Kango. [N3]
- **カロリー** — calorie (n). From English "calorie" (from Latin calor "heat"). Note: In nutrition, Japanese uses kcal (キロカロリー) but commonly shortens to カロリー. 1,800-2,000 "calories" in Japanese actually means kilocalories. [N2]
- **と言（い）われている** — is said to be (passive + progressive). From 言う [他動詞] + れる (passive) + ている (general belief). Indicates commonly accepted knowledge. [N4]

The number of applicants exceeded the quota.

---

- **志願者（しがんしゃ）** — applicant, volunteer (n). Kango. 志願 (volunteering/applying) + 者 (person). Distinguish from 志望者（しぼうしゃ）— 志願 implies formal application/enlistment, 志望 is more about hope/preference. [N2]
- **定員（ていいん）** — quota, capacity, authorized number (n). Kango. 定 (fixed) + 員 (member/personnel). [N2]
- **オーバー** — over, exceeding (n/suru-verb). From English "over." オーバーする = to exceed/go over. This is a suru-verb in Japanese: 定員をオーバーした. [N2]
- Note: This is another example of semantic narrowing. English "over" is a preposition/adverb, but Japanese オーバー is a noun/suru-verb meaning specifically "to exceed a limit." Related: オーバー気味 (tending to be excessive).

This machine is controlled by a computer.

---

- **機械（きかい）** — machine (n). Wago reading of 機械. [N4]
- **コンピューター** — computer (n). From English "computer." Often shortened to パソコン (personal computer) or PC. コンピューター is the general term. [N3]
- **コントロール** — control (n/suru-verb). From English "control." In this sentence, used in passive form: コントロールされている (is being controlled). [N2]
- **されている** — is being done (passive + progressive/state). コントロールする + れる (passive) + ている (ongoing state). [N4]
- Note: Japanese コントロール also appears in compounds: コントロールタワー (control tower), リモートコントロール (remote control). In gaming, コントローラー (controller) is the device.

The road curves sharply.

---

- **道（みち）** — road, path (n). Wago. [N5]
- **大きく（おおきく）** — greatly, sharply (adverbial form). From 大きい (i-adj). Here modifies the degree of curving. [N4]
- **カーブ** — curve (n/intransitive verb). From English "curve." In Japanese, カーブ can be a noun (a bend in the road) or a suru-verb (カーブする = to curve). Here used as カーブしている (is curving). [N2]
- Note: In baseball, カーブ means "curveball." The Japanese term for curve in a mathematical context is 曲線（きょくせん）. This polysemy — road bend, curveball, general curve — is specific to Japanese.

This road serves as the course for the citizens' marathon.

---

- **市民（しみん）** — citizen, public (n). Kango. 市民マラソン = a marathon open to the general public (not elite-only). [N3]
- **マラソン** — marathon (n). From English "marathon" (ultimately from Greek place name Μαραθών). [N3]
- **コース** — course, route (n). From English "course." In Japanese, コース covers: race course, golf course, set meal (コース料理), training program. [N2]
- **になっている** — has become, serves as (te-form + iru). になる indicates a state of being designated/functioning as something. [N5]
- Note: Japanese コース料理 (course meal) is a dining concept borrowed from Western multi-course dining. The Japanese set meal equivalent is 定食（ていしょく）.

I went to the velodrome to watch a race.

---

- **競輪場（けいりんじょう）** — velodrome (n). Kango. 競輪 (keirin = bicycle racing) + 場 (venue). 競輪 is a form of legalized gambling in Japan. [N2]
- **レース** — race (n). From English "race." In Japanese, レース covers: auto/bicycle/horse racing, and also lace (fabric) — a homonym from English "lace." Context determines meaning. [N2]
- **見（）にいった** — went to see (past). From 見る [他動詞] + 行く [自動詞]. 〜にいく = "go to do X." [N4]
- Note: The Japanese gambling context — 競輪 (keirin), 競馬（けいば, horse racing), 競艇（きょうてい, boat racing), オートレース (auto racing) — together form the "4公営ギャンブル" (four public gambling sports).

Country A leads the world in economics.

---

- **経済（けいざい）** — economy, economics (n). Kango. [N4]
- **世界（せかい）** — the world (n). Kango. [N4]
- **リード** — lead (n/suru-verb). From English "lead." リードする = to lead. 世界をリードしている = "leading the world." [N2]
- **している** — is doing (te-form + iru). Here indicates an ongoing state of leadership. [N5]
- Note: Japanese リード also means "leash" (dog leash = 犬のリード) from the same English word. The semantic range covers: (1) leadership, (2) physical lead/leash, (3) advantage in a game/score (リードしている = "is in the lead").

In the 100-meter race, I crossed the goal line in first place.

---

- **100メートル走（ひゃくメートルそう）** — 100-meter dash (n). メートル (meter) + 走 (race). [N3]
- **トップ** — top, first place (n). From English "top." In Japanese, トップでゴール = "to finish in first place." Also: トップになる (become number one), トップクラス (top-class). [N2]
- **ゴールイン** — to cross the finish line (n/suru-verb). From English "goal in" (Japanese coinage). ゴールインした = crossed the finish line. [N2]
- Note: トップ is a quintessential katakana word with broad usage: company president (トップ), top of a page (ページのトップ), top score (トップの成績).

Yamamoto finished the 100-meter backstroke with a new world record.

---

- **選手（せんしゅ）** — athlete, player (n). Kango. 選 (select) + 手 (hand/person). [N3]
- **100メートル背泳（せいえ）ぎ** — 100-meter backstroke (n). 背泳ぎ = backstroke. 背 (back) + 泳ぎ (swimming). [N2]
- **世界新記録（せかいしんきろく）** — new world record (n). Kango. 世界 (world) + 新 (new) + 記録 (record). [N2]
- **ゴール** — goal, finish (n/suru-verb). From English "goal." In Japanese, ゴールする can mean to finish a race (not just score in sports). ゴールした = finished/crossed the line. [N2]
- **で** — particle indicating means/manner. Here: "with" a new world record (as the manner of finishing). [N5]
- Note: In Japanese swimming terminology, the four strokes are: 自由（じゆう）泳ぎ (freestyle), 背泳ぎ (backstroke), 平泳（ひらおよ）ぎ (breaststroke), バタフライ (butterfly).

To pass a test.

---

- **テスト** — test, exam (n). From English "test." More casual than 試験（しけん）. [N4]
- **パス** — pass (n/suru-verb). From English "pass." パスする = to pass (a test). Note: パス can also mean "to pass/skip" (declining an offer: 今回はパスします) or "pass" in sports (パスを出す = to make a pass). [N2]
- **する** — to do (dictionary form). [N5]
- Note: The Chinese false friend is that パス does NOT mean "path" (路径). For path/route, Japanese uses 道（みち）, パス, or ルート (route). パス meaning "to skip/decline" is a uniquely Japanese usage: 「お茶でもどう？」「あ、今日はパス」—"How about some tea?" "Oh, I'll pass today."

This method is not the best, but it is fairly effective.

---

- **方法（ほうほう）** — method, way (n). Kango. [N4]
- **ベスト** — best (n/na-adj). From English "best." ベストではない = "is not the best." ベストを尽くす (do one's best) is a common phrase. [N2]
- **かなり** — fairly, considerably (adv). Wago. Indicates a significant degree, stronger than とても but less than 非常に. [N3]
- **効果（こうか）** — effect, effectiveness (n). Kango. 効果がある = "to be effective." [N3]
- **ある** — to exist, have (dictionary form). [N5]
- **〜が** — adversative conjunction. "X but Y." [N5]

I'm working hard to become a regular member of the (sports) team.

---

- **スポーツ** — sport(s) (n). From English "sports." [N3]
- **チーム** — team (n). From English "team." [N3]
- **レギュラー** — regular (member/player) (n). From English "regular." In sports, レギュラー = starting/regular player (as opposed to 補欠 ほけつ = substitute). Also: レギュラーサイズ (regular size), レギュラー放送 (regular broadcast). [N2]
- **なれるように** — so as to be able to become (volitional). From なれる (potential of なる) + ように (so that/in order to). [N4]
- **がんばっている** — am working hard (te-form + iru). From 頑張る [自動詞] "to do one's best." The ている form indicates ongoing effort. [N4]
- Note: Japanese レギュラー in the sports sense = "starter" in American English. British English might say "first team regular."

The coach of this judo club is famous for being strict.

---

- **柔道部（じゅうどうぶ）** — judo club (n). Kango. 柔道 (judo) + 部 (club/department). 部 refers to a school club. [N3]
- **コーチ** — coach (n). From English "coach." In Japanese, コーチ is used for sports coaches. For academic tutors, 先生（せんせい）or チューター is used. The manager/head coach is 監督（かんとく）. [N2]
- **厳（きび）しい** — strict, severe (i-adj). [N4]
- **こと** — nominalizer. Turns the adjective phrase 厳しい into a noun. [N5]
- **有名（ゆうめい）な** — famous (na-adj). Kango. 〜で有名だ = "is famous for." [N4]
- Note: Japanese distinguishes コーチ (coach, skill-focused) from 監督（かんとく）(manager/director, overall leadership) from トレーナー (trainer, fitness-focused).

A sports captain is expected to have a sense of responsibility and the ability to unite the team.

---

- **スポーツ** — sports (n). From English. [N3]
- **キャプテン** — captain (n). From English "captain." In Japanese school sports, the キャプテン is the team leader. The class captain is 学級委員（がっきゅういいん）or 委員長（いいんちょう）, not キャプテン. [N2]
- **責任感（せきにんかん）** — sense of responsibility (n). Kango. 責任 (responsibility) + 感 (feeling). [N2]
- **チームをまとめる** — to unite/bring together the team (noun-modifying phrase). まとめる [他動詞, counterpart: まとまる 自動詞] "to gather/unify/organize." [N3]
- **力（ちから）** — ability, power (n). Wago. [N5]
- **求（もと）められる** — is required, expected (passive). From 求める [他動詞] "to demand/seek." Passive: 〜は求められる = "X is expected/required of (someone)." [N3]
- Note: Japanese has multiple leadership terms: キャプテン (sports team leader), 主将（しゅしょう）(team captain, more formal), 監督（かんとく）(manager/coach), リーダー (general leader).

During my student days, I was in a drama club.

---

- **学生時代（がくせいじだい）** — student days, school days (n). Kango. 学生 (student) + 時代 (period/era). [N3]
- **演劇（えんげき）** — drama, theater (n). Kango. 演 (perform) + 劇 (drama). [N2]
- **サークル** — circle, club (n). From English "circle." In Japanese university context, サークル = an informal student club (as opposed to 部活 ぶかつ = official, school-recognized club). サークル is typically more casual and hobby-oriented. [N2]
- **入（はい）っていた** — was a member of, had joined (past progressive). From 入る [自動詞, counterpart: 入れる 他動詞] "to enter/join." 〜に入っていた = "was in/was a member of." [N4]
- Cultural note: The distinction between サークル (informal, student-run) and 部・部活 (formal, school-sanctioned with faculty advisor) is important in Japanese university culture.

This university's campus is rich in greenery.

---

- **大学（だいがく）** — university (n). Kango. [N5]
- **キャンパス** — campus (n). From English "campus" (originally Latin "field"). In Japanese, キャンパス refers specifically to a university campus (not a corporate or military one). [N2]
- **緑（みどり）** — green, greenery (n). Wago. 緑が豊か = "rich in greenery/lush." [N4]
- **豊（ゆた）か** — rich, abundant (na-adj). Wago. 緑が豊かだ = "lush with greenery." [N2]
- Note: Japanese universities with 緑が豊かなキャンパス are often associated with suburban or rural locations. Urban campuses (都心キャンパス) are a contrasting concept.

At the start of the new semester, there was an orientation for students about course registration.

---

- **新学期（しんがっき）** — new semester (n). Kango. 新 (new) + 学期 (semester). [N3]
- **学生（がくせい）** — student (n). Kango. 対象（たいしょう）= target audience. 学生を対象に = "targeting students / for students." [N4]
- **授業（じゅぎょう）登録（とうろく）** — course registration (n). Kango compound. 授業 (class/lesson) + 登録 (registration). [N2]
- **オリエンテーション** — orientation (n). From English "orientation." Often shortened to オリエン or オリ. In Japanese, specifically refers to new-student orientation or product orientation sessions. [N2]
- **あった** — there was, took place (past). From ある [自動詞] "to exist/to be held" (for events). [N5]

Classes are conducted according to the curriculum.

---

- **カリキュラム** — curriculum (n). From English "curriculum" (Latin "course, running"). In Japanese, カリキュラム refers to the organized set of courses in an educational program. カリキュラムに沿って = "according to/following the curriculum." [N2]
- **沿（そ）って** — along, according to (te-form). From 沿う [自動詞] "to run along/follow." 〜に沿って = "in accordance with." [N3]
- **授業（じゅぎょう）** — class, lesson (n). Kango. [N4]
- **行（おこな）う** — to conduct, carry out (dictionary form). 他動詞. Formal equivalent of する. [N3]
- Note: カリキュラム vs. シラバス (syllabus): カリキュラム is the overall program structure; シラバス is the per-course outline given to students.

Programs were distributed to the participants of the event.

---

- **大会（たいかい）** — tournament,大会, large event (n). Kango. [N3]
- **参加者（さんかしゃ）** — participant (n). Kango. 参加 (participation) + 者 (person). [N3]
- **プログラム** — program (n). From English "program." In this context, refers to a printed event program (schedule, performer list), NOT a computer program (which would also be プログラム but context distinguishes). [N2]
- **配（くば）られた** — were distributed (passive past). From 配る [他動詞, counterpart: 配られる (passive)] "to distribute/hand out." [N3]
- Note: Japanese プログラム covers: (1) event program (this sentence), (2) computer program, (3) TV program (テレビ番組 ばんぐみ). The computer sense is increasingly dominant in modern usage.

I attend piano lessons.

---

- **ピアノ** — piano (n). From English "piano" (shortened from pianoforte, Italian). [N5]
- **レッスン** — lesson (n). From English "lesson." In Japanese, レッスン is used for private/instructional lessons: piano lessons, dance lessons, etc. For school classes, 授業（じゅぎょう）is used. レッスンに通う = "attend lessons regularly." [N2]
- **通（かよ）う** — to commute, attend regularly (dictionary form). 自動詞. Implies regular, repeated travel to a location. [N3]
- Note: Japanese distinguishes: 授業 (school class), レッスン (private lesson/tutorial), 講座（こうざ）(course/lecture series), 講習（こうしゅう）(training course).

At the training camp, not only studying but also recreational activities are conducted.

---

- **合宿（がっしゅく）** — training camp, retreat (n). Kango. 合 (together) + 宿 (lodging). Common for sports teams, school clubs, and corporate training. [N2]
- **勉強（べんきょう）** — studying (n). Wago-derived (originally 勉強 meaning "endeavor/effort," semantic drift to "study"). [N4]
- **だけ** — only, just (particle). だけではなく = "not only... but also." [N4]
- **レクリエーション** — recreation (n). From English "recreation." Often shortened to レク. In Japanese, refers to organized recreational games/activities, especially in group settings like camps, hospitals, or elderly care. [N2]
- **行（おこな）われる** — is conducted, takes place (passive). From 行う [他動詞] "to conduct." The passive here indicates events happening in a general sense (not focusing on who organizes). [N3]

I go on a leisure trip abroad during the holidays.

---

- **休（やす）み** — holiday, vacation, day off (n). From verb 休む [自動詞, counterpart: 休ませる 他動詞] "to rest." [N5]
- **海外（かいがい）** — overseas, abroad (n). Kango. 海 (sea) + 外 (outside). [N3]
- **レジャー** — leisure (n). From English "leisure." In Japanese, レジャー specifically means recreational outings/activities: theme parks, resorts, sightseeing. レジャーに出かける = "go out for recreation." This is broader than English "leisure" (which is more abstract). [N2]
- **出（で）かける** — to go out (dictionary form). 自動詞, counterpart: 出かけさせる (causative). Implies going out for a purpose. [N4]
- Note: Japanese レジャー industry (レジャー産業) is a recognized economic sector, encompassing amusement parks, golf, pachinko, etc.

I work as a tour guide at a travel agency.

---

- **旅行会社（りょこうがいしゃ）** — travel agency (n). Kango. 旅行 (travel) + 会社 (company). [N3]
- **ガイド** — guide (n). From English "guide." In Japanese, ガイド covers: (1) tour guide (this sentence), (2) guidebook (ガイドブック), (3) user manual/instructions. The occupation is often ガイドさん. [N2]
- **している** — is doing, works as. する [他動詞]. 〜をしている for occupation. [N5]
- Note: For tour guide as a licensed profession, Japanese uses 通訳案内士（つうやくあんないし）(interpreter-guide, now 通訳案内業法). ガイド is the casual term.

In Japan, the period from December to February is the examination season.

---

- **日本（にほん）** — Japan (n). [N5]
- **12月（じゅうにがつ）から2月（にがつ）にかけて** — from December to February (phrase). 〜から〜にかけて = "from X to Y" (spanning a period). [N3]
- **受験（じゅけん）** — taking an examination (n). Kango. 受 (receive) + 験 (examine). 受験シーズン = exam season (a major cultural phenomenon in Japan, especially for university entrance exams). [N2]
- **シーズン** — season (n). From English "season." In Japanese, シーズン is used for: sports season, fashion season, and specific activity periods (受験シーズン, ボーナスシーズン). For natural seasons (spring/summer/etc.), 季節（きせつ）is used. [N2]

The train schedule was disrupted by an accident, but it was restored a few hours later.

---

- **事故（じこ）** — accident (n). Kango. [N4]
- **列車（れっしゃ）** — train (n). Kango. 列 (row/line) + 車 (vehicle). More formal than 電車. [N3]
- **ダイヤ** — timetable, schedule (n). Shortened from ダイヤグラム (diagram). ダイヤ refers specifically to train/bus timetables in Japanese (not diamonds, which are ダイヤモンド). ダイヤが乱れる = "schedule disrupted." [N2]
- **乱（みだ）れた** — was disrupted, became disordered (past). From 乱れる [自動詞, counterpart: 乱す 他動詞] "to become disordered." [N2]
- **数時間（すうじかん）後（ご）** — a few hours later (n). Kango. 数 (several) + 時間 (hours) + 後 (after). [N3]
- **復旧（ふっきゅう）** — restoration, recovery (n). Kango. 復旧する = to restore. [N2]
- Note: ダイヤ is one of the most distinctive Japanese transportation terms. ダイヤ改正 (timetable revision) happens several times a year on Japanese railways.

This road is congested on weekdays, but completely empty on holidays.

---

- **道路（どうろ）** — road (n). Kango. [N3]
- **ウィークデー** — weekday (n). From English "weekday." In Japanese, ウィークデー = Monday through Friday (business days). Often contrasted with 休日（きゅうじつ）or 週末（しゅうまつ）. Sometimes shortened to ウィークデイ. [N2]
- **渋滞（じゅうたい）** — traffic jam, congestion (n). Kango. 渋滞する = to be congested. [N2]
- **休日（きゅうじつ）** — holiday, day off (n). Kango. 休 (rest) + 日 (day). [N3]
- **がらがら** — empty, deserted (na-adj/adv). Mimetic word (擬態語). Describes a place with very few people. [N2]
- **だ** — copula. Plain form. [N5]
- Note: がらがら is also used for the sound of a rattling object (擬音語) — context distinguishes the "empty" vs. "rattling" meaning.

"Our company strives to provide service that will please our customers."

---

- **当社（とうしゃ）** — our company (n). Kango. 当 (this) + 社 (company). Humble/business term. [N2]
- **お客様（おきゃくさま）** — customer, client (n). Wago. お- + 客 + -さま. Triple honorific marking (お + 客 + さま) showing maximum politeness in business contexts. [N3]
- **喜（よろこ）ばれる** — to be pleased, delighted (passive). From 喜ぶ [自動詞] "to be glad." Passive: 〜に喜ばれる = "to please someone." [N3]
- **サービス** — service (n). From English "service." In Japanese, サービス also means: (1) freebie/complimentary item (サービスでつける = "throw in for free"), (2) discount (サービス価格), (3) in sports, a serve (tennis). [N2]
- **心（こころ）がけております** — we strive to, we make a point of (humble progressive). From 心がける [他動詞] "to keep in mind/endeavor." ております is humble form (kenjougo) of ている. [N2]
- Note: The Japanese サービス (freebie/discount) meaning is a uniquely Japanese semantic extension, not found in English. This is one of the most common 和製英語 usages.

Before the injection, I disinfect with alcohol.

---

- **注射（ちゅうしゃ）** — injection (n). Kango. 注 (pour) + 射 (shoot). 注射の前に = "before the injection." [N3]
- **アルコール** — alcohol (n). From English "alcohol" (ultimately Arabic الكحل). In Japanese, アルコール covers: (1) ethanol for disinfection (this sentence), (2) alcoholic beverages (アルコール飲料), (3) chemical alcohol. アルコール消毒（しょうどく）= alcohol disinfection. [N2]
- **消毒（しょうどく）** — disinfection (n). Kango. 消 (eliminate) + 毒 (poison/germ). 消毒する = to disinfect. [N2]
- **する** — to do. In the te-form here: して (implied before 消毒する in the sentence structure). [N5]
- Note: Japanese distinguishes アルコール (general alcohol) from エタノール (ethanol, specific chemical). For "alcoholic drinks," both アルコール and お酒（さけ）are used.

When December comes, many shops put up Christmas decorations.

---

- **12月（じゅうにがつ）** — December (n). [N5]
- **多く（おお）くの店（みせ）** — many shops (n phrase). 多くの = "many." [N4]
- **クリスマス** — Christmas (n). From English "Christmas." In Japan, Christmas is primarily a commercial/romantic celebration, not a religious one. [N3]
- **デコレーション** — decoration (n). From English "decoration." Often shortened to デコ. デコレーションする = to decorate. In Japanese, デコ also appears in デコトラ (decorated truck), デコスイーツ (decorated sweets). [N2]
- **する** — to do (dictionary form). [N5]
- **〜と** — conditional/temporal: "when X happens." 〜になると = "when it becomes X." [N4]
- Note: デコ is a productive prefix in modern Japanese: デコる (to decorate, suru-verb shortened), デコ電 (decorated cell phone — 2000s trend), デコピン (finger flick — unrelated etymology).
